claim: FAA maintains a Thermal Exhaust Plume Impact on Airport Operations technical guidance and assessment tool, based on MITRE's Exhaust-Plume-Analyzer, to evaluate whether exhaust/heat plumes pose a hazard to aircraft near airports.
source_title: Technical Guidance and Assessment Tool: Thermal Exhaust Plume Impact on Airport Operations
supporting_excerpt: FAA has produced 'Thermal Exhaust Plume Impact on Airport Operations: Technical Guidance and Assessment Tool'; MITRE developed the Exhaust-Plume-Analyzer tool available at no cost.
caveat: Direct FAA PDF fetch returned HTTP 403; content confirmed via FAA search snippet. FAA guidance is advisory, not a regulatory limit.

claim: A critical average vertical plume velocity of 4.3 m/s is used as the threshold above which an exhaust plume is considered a potential hazard to aircraft operations.
source_title: Assessment of the Risk to Aircraft from Stack Plume (Dr. Edward Porter, AWN) / CASA MOS Part 139 basis
supporting_excerpt: Part 139.370 of the Australian Civil Aviation Safety Regulations provides that plume velocities in excess of 4.3 m/s is or will be a potential hazard to aircraft operations.
airport_or_entity: CASA (Australia); applied methodology used in FAA/MITRE analyses
caveat: 4.3 m/s is explicitly a CASA (Australian) regulatory value; FAA applies same physics via its tool but treats it as advisory screening, not a codified U.S. limit.

claim: Significant turbulent effects from an exhaust plume can extend to heights of over 1,000 feet above the top of the stack or cooling tower.
source_title: FAA/MITRE thermal exhaust plume analysis (search summary of FAA guidance)
supporting_excerpt: Studies predict that the significant turbulent effects of an exhaust plume can extend to heights of over 1,000 feet above the height of the top of the stack or cooling tower.
denominator: height above top of stack/cooling tower
caveat: Drawn from FAA search snippet; FAA host blocked direct fetch. Verify page reference in source PDF.

claim: AC 150/5200-33C recommends a separation of 10,000 feet between an airport's aircraft movement areas and a hazardous wildlife attractant where turbine-powered aircraft are served, and 5,000 feet where only piston-powered aircraft are served.
source_title: AC 150/5200-33C, Hazardous Wildlife Attractants on or near Airports
page_or_section: separation criteria (10,000 ft turbine / 5,000 ft piston)
supporting_excerpt: New units located within 10,000 feet of any airport runway end used by turbojet aircraft, or within 5,000 feet of any airport runway end used only by piston-type aircraft, must demonstrate they are not hazards to aircraft.
denominator: distance from runway end / aircraft movement area to attractant
caveat: The 10,000/5,000 ft figures are also framed in EPA landfill-siting terms; confirm 33C's own separation-criteria section language and the 5-statute-mile perimeter provision in the source PDF (FAA host blocked direct fetch).

claim: Stormwater retention facilities with standing water are wildlife attractants; AC 150/5200-33 guidance recommends detention basins remain totally dry between rainfalls and that constant-flow basins use paved pads/ditches to prevent vegetation and nesting habitat.
source_title: AC 150/5200-33 series, Hazardous Wildlife Attractants on or near Airports
supporting_excerpt: Detention basins should remain totally dry between rainfalls; where constant flow is anticipated, the facility should include a concrete/paved pad and/or ditch/swale in the bottom to prevent vegetation that may provide nesting habitat.
caveat: Distinction matters: dry detention is acceptable; a wet retention pond is the disfavored design. Confirm exact section in 33C.

claim: Construction that penetrates 14 CFR Part 77 imaginary surfaces (including a 100:1 slope for 20,000 ft from the nearest runway) or exceeds 200 ft AGL must file FAA Form 7460-1 at least 45 days before construction, triggering an Obstruction Evaluation/Airport Airspace Analysis.
source_title: 14 CFR Part 77, Safe, Efficient Use, and Preservation of the Navigable Airspace
supporting_excerpt: If required to file notice under § 77.9, submit a completed FAA Form 7460-1 at least 45 days before the start date; any construction more than 200 ft AGL, or exceeding a 100:1 surface extending 20,000 ft from the nearest runway (longest runway >3,200 ft), must be reported.
denominator: distance from nearest runway; height AGL; days before construction
caveat: OE/AAA also evaluates ALP consistency and effects on NAVAIDs, radar, and cables beyond pure obstruction geometry.

claim: FAA Grant Assurances 19 (Operation and Maintenance), 20 (Hazard Removal and Mitigation), 21 (Compatible Land Use), 22 (Economic Nondiscrimination), and 29 (Airport Layout Plan) bind airport sponsors; 20 requires removing/mitigating hazards to approaches, 21 requires restricting incompatible adjacent land uses, and 29 bars changes inconsistent with the FAA-approved ALP without FAA approval.
source_type: FAA grant assurances (primary) with secondary summary
supporting_excerpt: 20: sponsor must remove, lower, light, or mark hazards threatening approaches. 21: restrict incompatible land uses around the airport. 29: keep an up-to-date ALP and not permit changes inconsistent with it without FAA approval.
caveat: Plain-language wording from avplot secondary summary; verify verbatim operative text against the AIP Sponsor Assurances PDF. Assurance 22 is weaker for this argument (obligates availability for aeronautical use).

claim: Airports are obligated to maintain a fee and rental structure that makes the airport as self-sustaining as possible, must charge fair market value for non-aeronautical land, and peers like DFW derive roughly 65% of revenue from non-aeronautical sources — so hosting revenue-generating tenants is FAA-encouraged in principle.
source_title: Navigating Airport Land Use Regulations to Grow Non-Aeronautical Revenue
page_or_section: non-aeronautical revenue and FAA fair-market-value requirement
supporting_excerpt: DFW generates nearly 65 percent of its revenue from non-aeronautical sources; FAA grant assurances prohibit airports from charging less than fair market value for non-aviation uses; FAA does not approve leases.
caveat: Counter-evidence to the memo: establishes that non-aero revenue is legitimate, so the argument must turn on siting/process, not on rejecting data centers outright.

claim: Virginia's Loudoun County 'Data Center Alley' — the world's largest data-center concentration — sits adjacent to IAD, with documented externalities including heat radiating from server halls and emissions from backup diesel generators.
source_title: Lessons for Delaware's future found in Virginia's Data Center Alley
page_or_section: environmental externalities of Data Center Alley
supporting_excerpt: Much of Virginia's data center hub sits in the vicinity of Dulles International Airport; harm comes from heat radiating from thousands of servers, emissions from backup diesel generators, and water pumped for cooling.
caveat: Journalistic source; establishes real-world adjacency and generation/heat externalities, not a specific plume measurement for the proposed parcel.

claim: AC 150/5190-4B governs airport land-use compatibility; changing a parcel to non-aeronautical use requires FAA consent/approval and, where the FAA holds ALP approval authority, a land-use change action.
source_title: AC 150/5190-4B, Airport Land Use Compatibility and Airport Land Use Planning; FAA Order 5190.6B Airport Compliance Manual
supporting_excerpt: Non-aeronautical uses are all uses not considered aeronautical or airport purpose; these uses require FAA consent or approval of the land use; the FAA has a land-use-change approval action for non-aeronautical uses where it holds ALP approval authority.
caveat: Confirms the process gap the memo identifies: a 2025 height/land-use screen is not the required ALP/land-use-change action. Verify exact AC 4B section language.
